newsitem.title: FRANCE: Galliano's couture for Dior sings ode to the muse.
newsitem.headline: Galliano's couture for Dior sings ode to the muse.

text.p: Amid palm fronds, rose bushes and tinkling fountains, the ghosts of Sarah Bernhardt, Isadora Duncan and Loie Fuller emerged in the fantastic creations of British designer John Galliano for Christian Dior on Tuesday.
Once again, the swashbuckling Briton surpassed himself with a triumphant haute couture collection gleaned from the slinky elegance of the Belle Epoque.

Duncan lived again in a stunning peacock gown, its design etched by slivers of fabric. Bernhardt was ever mysterious in pigeon-breasted black satin sparkling with jet embroidered bouquets while for Fuller in her boudoir, there was a hand-painted velvet robe edged with sable.

The supermodels turned out in full force in the steamy hothouse landscaped like a colonial garden in the deepest corners of exotica: Amber Valetta twirling the swelling skirts of a magnificent ballgown of black and gold organza ribbons, a saucy Naomi Campbell clad merely in the gold chains of a bayadere, or Shalom Harlow half-naked in a wisp of chiffon with roses tumbling down to her toes.

Embroidery that only miniature hands could have stitched swirled down the sleeves of corseted damask jackets with lace bustles in back. With these, the models wore lace stockings hitched to garter belts like the women in turn-of-the-century playboy reviews.

These were hardly garments for ordinary humans, although Galliano did keep society lunches in mind, sending out curvy tweed suits with enormous shawl collars over snake-like skirts that dragged along the floor. African-inspired silver hoop chokers elongated already swan-like necks.

"It was ravishing. A history of beautiful and seductive women from another time," said Joan Kaner of U.S. department store Neiman Marcus. "The workmanship was exquisite and the tweed suits are very wearable. I especially liked the shawl-collared herring bones. It was a dream."
Along with fellow-Londoner Alexander McQueen's startling and theatrical parade on Monday for Givenchy, Galliano's elegant ode to the muse left no doubt -- the Britons have conquered France.
"They're bringing such incredible energy to fashion. I think its great these houses have hired such controversial designers." said Nicole Fischelis of Saks Fifth Avenue department store.
This season's shows have also demonstrated that the elite couture club -- namely the two British designers -- has given up on politically correct fashion.
Snake and crocodile skins, sable, fox, mink and chinchilla, and feathers of all sorts have been proudly displayed on several catwalks since the season started on Sunday.
The Autumn-Winter couture collections continue through Thursday, with Christian Lacroix and Thierry Mugler finishing off the season.
